title: Genji-kō Poetry Exchange Pilot
description: A small, human-curated bank of connected waka for testing a sequential matching game, not a complete edition or a publication-ready critical text.
translation_credits: New provisional English game glosses drafted for this project; not taken from an existing published translation.

source_policy.poem_numbering: Global 1–795 order in the Kōi Genji Monogatari Text DB waka index
source_policy.original_text_note: Historical orthography is preserved from the public waka index, including variant kana, ditto marks, and manuscript-style spellings. Slashes separate the five verse units and are not in the source poem.
source_policy.caveat: Context, attribution, poem boundary, and response order require manual editorial confirmation in an annotated edition before final public release. Entries marked review_required must not be considered fully verified.

game_use.display_policy: Show only one poem at a time; hide chapter, exchange ID, speaker, recipient, motif labels, and pair order until the answer reveal.
game_use.pilot_pattern_recommendation: 2+2+1 or 2+1+1+1, because each exchange currently has exactly two poems.
constraints: For a five-card round, draw at most two poems from any exchange.
At most one copy of any poem may appear in a round.
Do not use chapter as the answer key; two independent exchanges can occur in one chapter.
Avoid selecting multiple pairs whose English glosses share an obvious keyword unless an intentionally hard round is being tested.
A solitary poem from an exchange is a legitimate singleton in a round; do not imply that every group must contain a pair.
All draft translations and answer explanations need Japanese-literary editorial review before assessment of player skill.

exchanges.context: An exchange recalled during the Rainy Night Discussion, in which a man and the woman he has been involved with contest whose conduct counts as a cause for separation.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The reply takes up the initiating poem's 'unhappy joints/occasions,' counting on the fingers, and the moment of parting; a rebuke becomes a counter-rebuke.

poems.speaker: Captain of the Left Horse (Sama no Kami), recounting an earlier relationship
poems.japanese: てをおりて/あひみし事を/かそふれは/これひとつやは/君かうきふし
poems.english_game_gloss: Counting on my fingers the times we have met, is this truly the only painful turn in your dealings with me?

poems.speaker: Woman in the Captain's anecdote
poems.japanese: うきふしを/心ひとつに/かそへきて/こや君かてを/わかるへきおり
poems.english_game_gloss: I have counted those painful turns alone in my heart; is this the moment when your own hand will let go of mine?

verification.review_note: The exchange is embedded in a character's anecdote rather than enacted in the novel's narrative present. The woman is unnamed.

exchanges.context: After Utsusemi evades Genji, the discarded cicada-shell robe becomes a token through which they articulate desire and concealment.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The answer repeats 'cicada' while reversing the perspective from a shell left behind to the hidden, tear-damp person.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: うつせみの/みをかへてける/木のもとに/なを人からの/なつかしきかな
poems.english_game_gloss: Beneath the tree where the cicada changed its body, I still find the empty shell of that person dear.

poems.speaker: Utsusemi
poems.japanese: うつせみの/はにをく露の/木かくれて/しのひ〱に/ぬるゝそてかな
poems.english_game_gloss: Like dew settling on a cicada's wing, hidden among the trees, my sleeves grow wet with secret tears.

verification.review_note: Genji's poem about the discarded robe is transmitted to Utsusemi, who appends her answer to the poem's paper; commentary identifies her answer as an adapted/quoted older poem.

exchanges.context: A woman associated with a house of evening-face flowers sends Genji a poem on a fan; he replies without openly naming himself.
exchanges.response_mechanism: Both use evening-face flowers and the uncertainty of identifying someone through pale light and twilight; the reply requests a closer view.

poems.speaker: Yūgao
poems.japanese: 心あてに/それかとそみる/しら露の/ひかりそへたる/ゆふかほの花
poems.english_game_gloss: I can only guess that it is you: the evening-face flower shines more brightly beneath the pale dew.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: よりてこそ/それかともみめ/たそかれに/ほの〱みつる/花のゆふかほ
poems.english_game_gloss: Only coming closer could I tell if it is truly you, the evening-face blossom I glimpsed faintly in twilight.

verification.review_note: Reply order has been explicitly corrected: the woman's fan-poem comes before Genji's answer.

exchanges.context: Murasaki's ailing grandmother wonders about the child's future; a woman of the household responds with a plea against dying too soon.
exchanges.response_mechanism: Young grass represents the child and vanishing dew represents the elder's mortality; the response turns an anxious image into an appeal to remain alive.

poems.speaker: Elder nun (Murasaki's grandmother)
poems.japanese: をひたゝむ/ありかもしらぬ/わか草を/をくらす露そ/きえんそらなき
poems.english_game_gloss: Not knowing where this young grass will grow to maturity, the dew that shelters it cannot bear to vanish.

poems.speaker: Lady attendant
poems.japanese: はつ草の/おひ行すゑも/しらぬまに/いかてか露の/きえんとすらむ
poems.english_game_gloss: Before you know where the new grass will grow, how can the dew think of disappearing?

verification.review_note: Annotated editions identify the speakers as the elder nun and an unnamed attendant; the child's fate motivates their imagery.

exchanges.context: At the Kamo festival, the older court lady Gen no Naishi makes a flirtatious pun on the aoi leaves worn by festival participants; Genji returns a pointed reply.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The word aoi evokes the ritual leaf and an 'occasion to meet'; both poems exploit the festival image to spar about attraction and exclusivity.

poems.speaker: Gen no Naishi
poems.japanese: はかなしや/人のかさせる/あふひゆへ/神のゆるしの/けふをまちける
poems.english_game_gloss: How futile to have waited for the god's sanctioned day, just for the aoi leaves another person wears—the day of meeting.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: かさしける/こゝろそあたに/おもほゆる/やそうち人に/なへてあふひを
poems.english_game_gloss: The heart that placed those leaves in the hair seems fickle to me—offering an aoi, a day of meeting, to every courtier alike.

verification.review_note: The aoi/au-hi pun is culturally specific and will require a player-facing hint or introduction.

exchanges.context: Genji addresses Princess Asagao with a respectful allusion to the ritual shoulder cord and a former bond; Asagao answers at a distance.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The answer echoes the initiator's 'that god/former time' and ritual yūdasuki, disputing what kind of remembered attachment is appropriate.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: かけまくは/かしこけれとも/その神の/あきおもほゆる/ゆふたすきかな
poems.english_game_gloss: It may be presumptuous even to speak of it, yet the sacred shoulder-cord draws my mind back to that god—and to old times.

poems.speaker: Princess Asagao
poems.japanese: その神や/いかゝはありし/ゆふたすき/心にかけて/しのふらんゆへ
poems.english_game_gloss: What was that god—or that former time—to you, that you should keep the ritual cord tied in your thoughts and long for it?

verification.review_note: Annotated editions confirm Genji and Princess Asagao. Interpretation of そのかみ ('long ago' / divine allusion) is pun-dependent; English is provisional.

exchanges.context: A visiting Gosechi dancer aboard a departing boat addresses the exiled Genji, who answers with the boat's motion and the waves at Suma.
exchanges.response_mechanism: A towline held by the music of a koto becomes an actual boat-rope and a figure of emotional hesitation; the answer sustains and redirects the maritime metaphor.

poems.speaker: Gosechi dancer
poems.japanese: ことのねに/ひきとめらるゝ/つなてなは/たゆたふ心/君しるらめや
poems.english_game_gloss: If the koto's sound holds me back like a towline, would you know how my heart hangs in hesitation?

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: こゝろありて/ひきてのつなの/たゆたはゝ/うちすきましや/すまのうら浪
poems.english_game_gloss: If the rope pulling your boat truly wavered out of feeling, could it simply pass beyond the waves of Suma?

verification.review_note: A previously tested pairing; boat/towline imagery is strong when the English gloss preserves it.

exchanges.context: Genji hopes for an intimate companion with whom to discuss his dreamlike misfortunes; the Akashi lady counters that she cannot tell waking from dream.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The answer repeats the metaphor of a dream but replaces Genji's wish for a companion with the respondent's inability to distinguish reality from illusion.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: むつことを/かたりあはせむ/人もかな/うき世の夢も/なかはさむやと
poems.english_game_gloss: If only I had someone with whom to share intimate words—perhaps I might wake halfway from this bitter world's dream.

poems.speaker: Lady of Akashi
poems.japanese: あけぬ夜に/やかてまとへる/心には/いつれを夢と/わきてかたらむ
poems.english_game_gloss: My heart is lost in a night that never dawns; how could I tell which part is dream and put it into words?

verification.review_note: The historical transcription なかはさむ corresponds to the edited なかば覚む ('wake partway'); the English gloss makes that interpretation explicit.

exchanges.context: Genji sends a farewell to a woman connected with the court, who suspects that his regret at parting is a pretext for a different attachment.
exchanges.response_mechanism: Both poems turn explicitly on the word 'parting,' but the response reinterprets the sender's regret as an excuse rather than shared sorrow.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.recipient: Daughter of a court lady referred to as Senji
poems.japanese: かねてより/へたてぬ中と/ならはねと/わかれはおしき/物にそありける
poems.english_game_gloss: Though we were never accustomed to an intimacy without distance, I have learned that parting is painful all the same.

poems.speaker: Daughter of a court lady referred to as Senji
poems.japanese: うちつけの/わかれをおしむ/かことにて/おもはむかたに/したひやはせぬ
poems.english_game_gloss: Is your sudden lament at parting only a pretext, so that you may follow wherever your heart truly wishes to go?

verification.review_note: The addressee is a daughter of a former palace attendant called Senji (宣旨); her name is not given. The dialogue is linked to a court appointment/parting.

exchanges.context: Genji visits Suetsumuhana's neglected dwelling, where wisteria and waiting frame the uneasy reunion.
exchanges.response_mechanism: Both play on matsu ('pine' and 'to wait') and the lingering house; the reply questions whether the caller came for the woman or merely the flowers.

poems.speaker: Hikaru Genji
poems.japanese: ふちなみの/うちすきかたく/みえつるは/まつこそやとの/しるしなりけれ
poems.english_game_gloss: I could hardly pass by these waves of wisteria; they must be the sign of a house that has waited for me.

poems.speaker: Suetsumuhana
poems.japanese: としをへて/まつしるしなき/わかやとを/花のたよりに/すきぬはかりか
poems.english_game_gloss: For years my house has waited without a sign of reward; have you only stopped by because the flowers gave you a reason?

verification.review_note: English reveals a portion of the matsu pun; consider a glossary for Japanese-advanced mode.

exchanges.context: Murasaki no Ue and Akikonomu exchange poems in the seasonal contest between spring flowers and autumn insects.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The response picks up the butterfly carried by the first poem while placing an obstacle of thick yamabuki flowers between sender and recipient.

poems.speaker: Murasaki no Ue
poems.japanese: はなそのゝ/こてふをさへや/したくさに/秋まつむしは/うとくみるらむ
poems.english_game_gloss: Would even a butterfly from the flower garden seem a stranger to the autumn-crickets waiting deep among the grasses?

poems.speaker: Akikonomu (the Autumn Princess)
poems.japanese: こてふにも/さそはれなまし/こゝろありて/やへ山ふきを/へたてさりせは
poems.english_game_gloss: I might gladly follow even a butterfly, if only those layers of golden kerria blossoms did not keep us apart.

verification.review_note: The word kochō ('butterfly') carries an additional pun on 'come here,' and yamabuki is kerria; the English gloss does not fully capture the wordplay.

exchanges.context: Kaoru's approach to the Uji sisters is expressed through boatmanship and river imagery, answered by the elder sister's image of sleeves worn away by spray.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The river-pole's dripping water is reimagined as the constant moisture of tears and the wearing down of sleeves; the response sustains the Uji river setting.

poems.speaker: Kaoru
poems.japanese: 橋ひめの/心をくみて/たかせさす/さほのしつくに/袖そぬれぬる
poems.english_game_gloss: Trying to fathom the lady at the bridge, I dip my pole into the shallows; its falling drops have soaked my sleeves.

poems.speaker: Ōigimi (elder Uji princess)
poems.japanese: さしかへる/うちの河おさ/あさ夕の/しつくや袖を/くたしはつらむ
poems.english_game_gloss: Pushing back and forth along the Uji River, will the drops of morning and evening wear your sleeves away entirely?

verification.review_note: The river-steering technical vocabulary may need a short glossary to distinguish imagery from ordinary repeated words.

exchanges.context: The Eighth Prince, separated from visitors by river and mountain mist, sends a verse that Niou answers on Kaoru's behalf.
exchanges.response_mechanism: Distant white waves and a wind that clears clouds or mist are turned into a plea for the Uji river wind to cross the intervening space.

poems.speaker: Eighth Prince (Hachi no Miya)
poems.japanese: 山風に/かすみふきとく/こゑはあれと/へたてゝみゆる/をちのしら浪
poems.english_game_gloss: The mountain wind can be heard blowing the mist apart, yet the white waves across the distance still seem to keep us apart.

poems.speaker: Niou (replying for Kaoru's party)
poems.japanese: をちこちの/汀になみは/へたつとも/なをふきかよへ/うちの河風
poems.english_game_gloss: Though waves separate the shores on either side, keep blowing between us, wind over the Uji River.

verification.review_note: Composing the reply on behalf of another person is pedagogically useful; retain it as author/role metadata but hide it during a round.

exchanges.context: Niou inquires about the autumn mountain village in a poem addressed to Naka no Kimi; Ōigimi composes a reply for her sister.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The first verse's deer, mountain village, and dew are transformed into a chorus of deer at the fence and a mountain village veiled in tears and mist.

poems.speaker: Niou
poems.japanese: をしかなく/秋の山さと/いかならむ/こ萩か露の/かゝる夕くれ
poems.english_game_gloss: What must the autumn mountain village be like this evening, as deer call and dew gathers on the little bush clover?

poems.speaker: Ōigimi (composing for Naka no Kimi)
poems.japanese: なみたのみ/きりふたかれる/山里は/まかきに鹿そ/もろこゑになく
poems.english_game_gloss: In this mountain village shrouded in a mist of tears, the deer at the fence cry out together, voice answering voice.

verification.review_note: Two different exchanges from the same chapter occur in this pilot, a useful check against inadvertently treating chapter as group ID.

exchanges.context: Kaoru proposes a durable bond to Ōigimi by invoking a knot; she counters with the image of fragile, tear-strung pearls.
exchanges.response_mechanism: The reply directly repeats a 'long promise' but argues that it cannot be tied on a strand made fragile by tears, overturning the knot of the first verse.

poems.speaker: Kaoru
poems.japanese: あけまきに/なかき契を/むすひこめ/おなしところに/よりもあはなむ
poems.english_game_gloss: Let us tie a long promise into the trefoil knot, our strands coming together at a single place.

poems.speaker: Ōigimi (elder Uji princess)
poems.japanese: ぬきもあへす/もろき涙の/たまのをに/なかき契を/いかゝむすはん
poems.english_game_gloss: On a fragile string of tear-pearls I cannot even thread together, how could I tie a promise that must last so long?

verification.review_note: Strong matching potential, but translation should preserve the knot/string contrast, not just generic promises.
